\chapter{Five Words for Eating Out}
\label{ch:el-menu-y-el-camarero}
\hlchaptermodality{391}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say el menú, el camarero, el postre, el supermercado and el euro, and name five things I meet when I eat out.}

Complete ES-C391-euro: name five things I meet when I eat out, and say one thing about each.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el menú]{el menú — one Latin word, three Spanish arrivals}

\label{lesson:ES-C391-menu}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the elevator}, then \emph{the swimming pool}. (\emph{El ascensor}; \emph{la piscina}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la carta — the other thing a restaurant hands you.
  \item el restaurante — where both arrive.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{me-NÚ}, two beats with the weight on the second. The written accent is there to say so; without it the eye would fall on the first beat instead. The \emph{u} is a tight \emph{oo}, held short, and the \emph{n} is a plain \emph{n}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el menú} — the meal a kitchen has already decided on, written out.

Spanish took the word from French \textbf{menu}, and in French it was a describing word before it was anything else: small, detailed, fine-grained. A \emph{menu} list was a list broken down small. Behind the French sits Latin \textbf{minūtus}, made small, from \textbf{minuere}, to lessen.

The stress is the proof, and it is the kind of proof you can hear. Spanish says \emph{me-NÚ}, weight on the last beat, exactly where French puts it. A word carried down out of Latin by mouth would not have landed there.

That is worth pressing, because \emph{minūtus} reached Spanish twice more, by two other roads:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{menudo} — carried down by mouth, worn short, everyday;
  \item \textbf{minuto} — lifted out of writing, its Latin shape kept whole;
  \item \textbf{menú} — handed over by French, keeping the French weight on the end.
\end{itemize}

Three words, three shapes, one Latin word. English holds the same root in \textbf{minute}, \textbf{diminish}, \textbf{minor}, \textbf{minus} and \textbf{mince}, and borrowed the list itself in 1837 as \textbf{menu}.

Now the warning, which will cost you a meal if you skip it. In Spain, \emph{el menú} normally names the fixed set meal — the \textbf{menú del día}, one price, the courses chosen by the kitchen. The list you order freely from is \textbf{la carta}. Ask for \emph{el menú} expecting the second, and the first is what arrives.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name what the kitchen has already decided on: \emph{el menú}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el menú}
  \item \emph{el menú del día}
\end{itemize}

Now three in a row: \emph{el ascensor}, \emph{la piscina}, \emph{el menú}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of \emph{menudo}, \emph{minuto} and \emph{menú} came in through French? (\emph{Menú} — the final stress is the tell.) In Spain, which one is the fixed meal of the day, \emph{el menú} or \emph{la carta}? (\emph{El menú}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el camarero]{el camarero — the servant of a room, at your table}

\label{lesson:ES-C391-camarero}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the swimming pool}, then \emph{the set meal of the day}. (\emph{La piscina}; \emph{el menú del día}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el restaurante — where you will say it.
  \item el cuarto — a room, which is where this word started.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ca-ma-RE-ro}, four beats with the weight on the third. The \emph{c} before \emph{a} is a hard \emph{k}. Both \emph{r}s are single quick taps of the tongue tip, nothing rolled. Both \emph{a}s are wide open and equal, the unstressed one no fainter than the other. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el camarero} — the person who takes your order and brings your food.

Underneath it sits \textbf{cámara}, a room. That goes back to Greek \textbf{kamára}, a vault or vaulted chamber, which Latin took as \textbf{camera}.

One small thing in the shape is worth catching. Spanish has \emph{cámara}, with an \textbf{a} in the middle — matching the everyday Latin \textbf{camara}, not the classical \textbf{camera} with its \textbf{e}. The word came up through speech, not off the page. Corominas finds \emph{cámara} in Spanish already in the \emph{Cid}.

English has that room twice over: \textbf{chamber} and \textbf{camera} are one Latin word arriving by two routes, and \textbf{bicameral}, a state with two chambers, keeps the plain sense.

Now the part where care is owed, because the sources split and neither is careless:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Wiktionary derives \emph{camarero} from Medieval Latin \textbf{camarārius};
  \item Corominas keeps it at home — Spanish \emph{cámara} with the ending \textbf{-ero} on it, dated 1206.
\end{itemize}

Both roads end at exactly the word Spanish has. There is no crack of sound or spelling between them to prise apart, so the honest answer is not one of the two — it is that they cannot be told apart.

Two near-misses to refuse. English \textbf{chamberlain} looks like a cousin and is not: it is \emph{camera} with a Germanic ending instead of the Spanish one, built alongside \emph{camarero} rather than before it. And \textbf{camarón}, a shrimp, has nothing to do with any of this — different Latin word, \emph{cammarus}.

One more honesty. When and how the servant of a chamber became the person who brings your dinner is not something the sources record. You will see confident centuries quoted for it; none is offered here.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name the person who serves you: \emph{el camarero}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el camarero}
  \item \emph{el camarero trae el menú}
\end{itemize}

Now three in a row: \emph{la piscina}, \emph{el menú}, \emph{el camarero}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{cámara} name before anything else? (A room — and before that, a vault.) Can anyone say whether \emph{camarero} was made inside Spanish or borrowed from Medieval Latin? (No. Both roads arrive at the same word.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el postre]{el postre — a word cut out of the middle of a phrase}

\label{lesson:ES-C391-postre}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the set meal of the day}, then \emph{the waiter}. (\emph{El menú del día}; \emph{el camarero}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item dulce — what it usually is.
  \item la fruta — what it often was.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{POS-tre}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{s} stays a clean hiss and never buzzes into a \emph{z}. The \emph{t} is made with the tongue against the back of the teeth, drier than an English \emph{t}, and the \emph{r} behind it is one quick tap. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el postre} — dessert; the last thing brought to the table.

The family is Latin \textbf{post}, after, with \textbf{posterus}, following, and \textbf{postrēmus}, last, standing behind it. That much is firm. Almost nothing after it is, and this is a word where you should be told so.

Corominas, who is the careful one here, does not make \emph{postre} something Spanish inherited. He makes it something Spanish \textbf{cut out of a phrase it already had}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{a la postre} — in the end, finally;
  \item then \textbf{fruta de postre} — the fruit that comes at the end;
  \item then \emph{postre} standing alone as the dish itself, documented in 1561.
\end{itemize}

That is why the word looks like a fragment. It is one. It was carved out of the middle of a fixed expression and left to stand up by itself.

And he does not stop hedging there. The \emph{postrero} underneath \emph{a la postre} he calls \emph{más dudosa} — more doubtful — offering only that it \textbf{probably} arose from a crossing of \emph{postremo} with the words that meant much the same thing: \emph{cabero}, \emph{trasero}, \emph{derradero}. Probably. He says no more, and neither will this page.

You will meet tidier accounts of \emph{postre} than this, printed with no hedge at all. Refuse them. The neatest of them rests on a Latin expression that no source attests — reverse-engineered so that it produces the dessert, which is the one thing it was built to produce.

The English relatives are \textbf{posterior}, \textbf{posterity} and plain \textbf{post-}. The best of them is \textbf{preposterous}: \emph{prae}, before, plus \emph{posterus}, after. It means back-to-front because it says back-to-front. English \textbf{poster} is no relation whatever.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name the last course of the meal: \emph{el postre}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el postre}
  \item \emph{el postre es dulce}
\end{itemize}

Now three in a row: \emph{el menú}, \emph{el camarero}, \emph{el postre}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which phrase was \emph{postre} cut out of? (\emph{A la postre}, finally — then \emph{fruta de postre}, and then the dish on its own.) Is \emph{postre} any relation to English \emph{poster}? (None at all.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el supermercado]{el supermercado — an English shop, rebuilt out of Spanish parts}

\label{lesson:ES-C391-supermercado}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the waiter}, then \emph{the dessert is sweet}. (\emph{El camarero}; \emph{el postre es dulce}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el mercado — the half you already have.
  \item la tienda — the smaller shop beside it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{su-per-mer-CA-do}, five beats with the weight on the fourth. The opening \emph{s} is a clean hiss. Both \emph{r}s are quick taps, not rolls. The \emph{c} before \emph{a} is a hard \emph{k}, and the \emph{d} of \emph{-ado} is barely closed at all — the tongue brushes the teeth, nearer the \emph{th} of English \emph{this} than a full \emph{d}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el supermercado} — a supermarket.

The two halves of this word are separated by roughly two thousand years, and that gap is the whole lesson.

The back half is ancient and came in by mouth. Latin \textbf{mercātus} was a trading, from \textbf{mercārī}, to trade, from \textbf{merx, mercis}, wares. Centuries of speech wore it down into \textbf{mercado}, and nobody sat down to make it. English took the same root by other doors: \textbf{market}, \textbf{merchant}, \textbf{mercantile}, \textbf{merchandise}, \textbf{commerce}, and the name \textbf{Mercury}.

The front half is younger than most people's grandparents. American English coined \textbf{supermarket} in 1933 — and Spanish did not take the English word. It translated it, piece against piece: \emph{super} onto \emph{super}, \emph{market} onto \emph{mercado}. A word built that way has a name. It is a \textbf{calque}: the foreign pattern crosses the border while the foreign sounds stay home.

Set the two ways in beside each other. A borrowed word arrives with its foreignness showing, and you can often hear where it came from. A calque arrives invisible — Spanish material throughout, Spanish stress, nothing to hear — and you would never guess it had been abroad unless someone told you.

One caution, because this move gets over-used. \emph{Supermercado} really is a calque, and a dictionary says so, which is why it can be stated flatly here. The same tidy story gets told about \emph{aeropuerto} — air plus port, copied straight from English — and there the claim is not actually supported by the sources. A word that \textbf{looks} assembled has not thereby been shown to be assembled.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name where the food comes from before it reaches the table: \emph{el supermercado}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el supermercado}
  \item \emph{el supermercado está cerca}
\end{itemize}

Now three in a row: \emph{el camarero}, \emph{el postre}, \emph{el supermercado}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which half of \emph{supermercado} was carried down by mouth from Latin? (\emph{Mercado}.) What does calling the word a calque claim about it? (Its parts were translated one for one instead of borrowed — an English pattern in Spanish material.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el euro]{el euro — a coin cut out of a longer word}

\label{lesson:ES-C391-euro}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the dessert}, then \emph{the supermarket is nearby}. (\emph{El postre}; \emph{el supermercado está cerca}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el dinero — money in general.
  \item la moneda — the coin in your hand.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{EU-ro}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{e} and the \emph{u} run together inside that one beat, both still audible, an \emph{eh} sliding into an \emph{oo} in the time of a single vowel. The \emph{r} is one tap; the final \emph{o} stays round and full. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el euro} — the currency.

Open the Academy's dictionary at \emph{euro} and find two entries, not one — and not the same word.

The first is Latin \textbf{eurus}, from Greek \textbf{euros} — a poetic name for one of the cardinal winds. The second is the money. Four shared letters, nothing else.

This matters, because the wind is the tempting answer: old, Greek, the better story, and sitting in the dictionary looking like an ancestor. Any account of the currency that opens \textquotedblleft{}from the Greek\textquotedblright{} has changed the subject to weather.

The money is plainer than that. It is a longer word cut short — and the Academy cuts it from \textbf{europeo}, not from \emph{Europa}. A small divergence from the usual telling, worth keeping: it is what the dictionary prints — the describing word clipped, not the name of the continent.

The name itself was settled at the European Council in Madrid, in December 1995.

Who first thought of it is where the record thins. The coinage is widely attributed to \textbf{Germain Pirlot}, a Belgian teacher, in a letter written that year. Hold that as an attribution rather than a fact: Wiktionary itself calls it \emph{the official story}, the priority rests on Pirlot's own statement that he knew of nobody proposing it earlier, and etymonline names no coiner whatever. Somebody wrote the word down first; whether it was him is not settled.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name five things you meet when you eat out: \emph{el menú}, \emph{el camarero}, \emph{el postre}, \emph{el supermercado}, \emph{el euro}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el euro}
  \item \emph{pago con euros}
\end{itemize}

Now all five together. Name each thing, then say one thing about it.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el menú — el menú está en la mesa}
  \item \emph{el camarero — el camarero trae el agua}
  \item \emph{el postre — el postre es dulce}
  \item \emph{el supermercado — el supermercado está cerca}
  \item \emph{el euro — pago con euros}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does the Academy's dictionary take the currency's name from? (From \emph{europeo}, clipped short — not from the Greek wind, a separate entry and a separate word.) Is Germain Pirlot documented as the coiner? (No — it is an attribution, and one reference names nobody at all.)
\end{tcolorbox}
